title: Echo Weaver Starts Its Endless Time Loop With Release Trailer
excerpt: A 2D metroidvania that's less about gaining new skills as learning what you can do, because a time loop doesn't allow for bringing anything back.
content:
Published Oct 9, 2026, 4:24 AM EDT

James grew up in the arcades of the 80s and has played games on everything from the Milton Bradley Microvision to the PlayStation 5. He worked in gaming retail during the PS1/PS2 eras, and even had a small stint at Working Designs. It's been a very long ride and is nowhere even close to over yet, and every stop along the way is a chance for something new and fascinating to emerge. Whether that be on a mainstream console like the now-classic Xbox 360 or something less obvious such as PlayDate or NeoGeo Pocket Color, it's all worth looking at.

Granted, what's worth looking at is defined by personal taste, and in James' case that tends to be more mechanics-oriented games rather than narrative ones. Fast action shooters such as Dusk are as good as more meticulous games like Satisfactory, but there's always room for a good action RPG too. Most importantly is always looking to see what's new, because as nice as the past was and as important as it is to not forget it, getting mired down in what one knows is a great way to stagnate. There's too much amazing gaming being created on a near-daily basis to settle for what you know.

Every day begins the same, except every day is actually the same day. A long drop into a half-temple, half-sewer, standing up with no memory how how this all started, and one single minute on the clock to figure it all out before the time loop starts over. It's not a lot to work with but still beats having no time all, and every trip into the loop gives new memories to help get a little father the next time around. The world resets but memory doesn't, and the Weaver is far more skilled than he realizes when the first loop begins.

Its Like Having All the Time In the World Via High-Efficiency Temporal Recycling

Echo Weaver released today on PC and consoles, and it's a 2D metroidvania that's not so much about gaining abilities and upgrades as learning what you can do, because a time loop doesn't allow for bringing anything back to its beginning. The Weaver will be the same enigmatic white-haired boy he was at the start of the game, but you'll be aware of the things he's learned during the previous run. How various skills fit together, shortcuts through the environment, when to walk back to where you left off on the previous run and when to take warp to a checkpoint, etc. No matter how you approach it, though, you'll want to be efficient about it.

At the start of each run there's no more than a single minute on the clock before time slows down and the Weaver is thrown back to the start of the loop. Thankfully it's not a hard limit, with the big crystals in the environment adding a minute apiece to the clock. Because the levels reset the crystals are always available again on the next run, and it doesn't take more than a bit of exploring a new area to remember where they are and chart a path that gives plenty of time for exploration. There are more than a few secrets to chase after, and dying by lack of health is far more common than running out of time.

While there is a bit of combat in the game, Echo Weaver is mostly a platformer at heart and takes serious acrobatics to survive. The Weaver finds a glaive early in the adventure, as useful for tagging door switches as it is for enemies, but the run & jump is the main aspect of the game. The Weaver's abilities expand as new environmental objects get added to the world, allowing him to multi-jump through treetops, zip along from one glowing orb to the next, or teleport to his glaive, and the puzzles focus not only on using the full skillset but also knowing which ones to leave aside. More than a few optional areas require figuring out the right combination of moves, with the wrong one breaking the puzzle and requiring a reset back to the sewer-temple to start again. Add in gates that start closing the second the run begins and you'll be restarting more than a few rounds to chase after Echo Weaver's secrets.

The problem with describing a game like Echo Weaver is that a large part of it is discovering what you can do, which is very different from the standard "reach checkpoint, unlock skill". Explaining a jumping puzzle and the moves needed to get through it becomes spoiler territory, rather than an overview of the game mechanics, and a big part of the fun is finding environmental objects that turn out to be more than just decoration, or that certain skills are far more significant than they looked. For every standard gaming mechanic like checkpoints you can warp to directly at the start of the run there are secret abilities, hidden routes, and even a few less critical moves that aren't strictly necessary but are still left for the player to figure out. Every new run of Echo Weaver starts right back where the first one began, and the most effective power-up the Weaver earns is the knowledge of the skills he already has.
